## Objectives

- Outward vs inward FDI
- Identify barriers to inward FDI
- Compare commercial and strategic investment logic against official development assistance (ODA)

## Key Concepts

- Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)
- Mergers & Acquisitions (M&A)
- Multinational Enterprises (MNEs)

## Roadmap

- Concepts: FDI, M&A, MNEs
- Trends: Japanese outward FDI to ASEAN, manufacturing and services
- Barriers: what holds back inward FDI
- Logic: commercial and strategic investment vs. ODA

## Overview: FDI and ODA
```{r}
world = fread("../data/08 fdi/world_fdi_oda.csv")
world[, indicator := fcase(
  indicator == "Foreign direct investment, net inflows", "FDI inflows",
  indicator == "Net official development assistance and official aid received", "ODA and official aid",
  indicator == "Personal remittances, received", "Remittances",
  default = indicator)]
ggarrange(
  ggline(world[!grepl("outflows",indicator)],
         x="date",xlab="",
         numeric.x.axis = T,
         y="value",ylab="value (current US$)",
         color = "indicator",
         caption = "Source: World Bank") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-12, suffix = "tr")),
  ggline(world[!grepl("outflows",indicator)],
         x="date",xlab="",
         numeric.x.axis = T,
         y="gdp_share",ylab="GDP share (%)",
         color = "indicator",
         caption = "Source: World Bank") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 100, suffix = "%")),
  common.legend = TRUE, legend = "bottom"
)
```

::: notes
- Recap of lecture 1: ODA is public, concessional, development-oriented.
- Today: FDI is private and profit-seeking; compare scale and GDP share.
:::

## Key concepts: FDI, M&A, MNEs

- FDI: cross-border investment with a lasting interest and control (commonly a 10% voting-share threshold)
  - Forms: greenfield, M&A, reinvested earnings
- M&A: acquiring or merging with an existing foreign firm, rather than building new capacity
- MNEs: firms that own and control operations in more than one country; the main actors behind FDI
- Motives: market-seeking, resource-seeking, efficiency-seeking

## FDI vs. portfolio investment

- **Direct investment:** lasting interest and influence over management of a foreign enterprise (typically 10% or more of voting power).
- **Portfolio investment:** cross-border holdings of securities without a direct-investment relationship.
- Direct investment is closely linked to multinational production and global value chains; portfolio flows are generally more liquid and volatile.

::: notes
- In the balance of payments, both direct and portfolio investment are recorded in the financial account.
- The Balance of Payments lecture shows that Japan's portfolio flows have been more volatile than direct investment flows.
:::

## Why do countries want inward FDI?

<div class="slide-font-size" style="--slide-font-size: 80%">

- **Capital:** finance factories, equipment, and business expansion.
- **Jobs and income:** create employment and demand for domestic suppliers.
- **Technology and skills:** introduce production methods, management practices, and worker training.
- **Export opportunities:** connect domestic production to multinational firms' international networks.
- **Productivity and growth:** domestic firms may benefit through learning and supplier relationships.

Benefits are not automatic: local skills and firms' ability to absorb technology matter.

</div>

::: notes
- Borensztein, De Gregorio, and Lee (1998) emphasize the role of human capital in realizing growth benefits from FDI: https://www.nber.org/papers/w5057
- Javorcik (2004) finds evidence consistent with productivity spillovers to domestic suppliers in Lithuania: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0002828041464605
:::

## Japan's direct investment: Outward vs. inward

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Units: assumed 100 million yen (BOJ/MOF convention); dividing by 1e4 gives trillion yen. Confirm against the source.
boj = fread("../data/08 fdi/boj_investment.csv")
setnames(boj, c("year", "Direct_out", "Portfolio_out", "Direct_in", "Portfolio_in"))
boj = boj[grepl("^[0-9]{4}$", year)]
boj = boj[, lapply(.SD, as.numeric)]
bcols = setdiff(names(boj), "year")
boj[, (bcols) := lapply(.SD, function(x) x / 1e4), .SDcols = bcols]
boj_di = melt(boj[, .(year, Outward = Direct_out, Inward = Direct_in)],
              id.vars = "year", variable.name = "Direction")

ggline(boj_di,
       x = "year", xlab = "",
       numeric.x.axis = T,
       y = "value", ylab = "Trillion yen",
       color = "Direction",
       legend = "bottom",
       caption = "Source: Bank of Japan, Balance of payments") +
  theme(legend.title = element_blank())
```

::: notes
- Cumulative 1996–2025: outward roughly 370 trillion yen vs. inward roughly 58 trillion yen (about 6x), assuming units of 100 million yen.
- Japan is a large net outward investor; inward FDI stays small relative to GDP. Use this to lead into "barriers to inward FDI".
:::

## Where does Japanese FDI go?

```{r}
#| include: false
fdi_2024 = fread("../data/08 fdi/japan_fdi_by_country_industry_2024.csv")
japan_destinations = fdi_2024[direction == "Outward"]
asean_total = japan_destinations[destination == "ASEAN" & industry == "Total", value_100million_yen]
world_total = japan_destinations[destination == "World" & industry == "Total", value_100million_yen]
asean_world_share = 100 * asean_total / world_total

# Reuse the same country/industry definition and source totals in both charts.
fdi_destination_plot = function(countries, divisor, unit_label, subtitle, accuracy) {
  totals = japan_destinations[destination %in% countries & industry == "Total"]
  setorder(totals, value_100million_yen)
  dat = japan_destinations[destination %in% countries &
                            industry %in% c("Manufacturing", "Non-manufacturing")]
  dat[, destination := factor(destination, levels = totals$destination)]
  totals[, destination := factor(destination, levels = levels(dat$destination))]
  dat[, industry := factor(industry, levels = c("Manufacturing", "Non-manufacturing"))]
  ggplot(dat, aes(destination, value_100million_yen / divisor, fill = industry)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.65, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
    geom_text(data = totals,
              aes(destination, value_100million_yen / divisor,
                  label = label_number(accuracy = accuracy, big.mark = ",")(value_100million_yen / divisor)),
              inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = -0.12, size = 5) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Manufacturing" = "#4477AA", "Non-manufacturing" = "#DDCC77")) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.16))) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = paste0("Annual net outward FDI (", unit_label, ")"), fill = NULL,
         subtitle = subtitle,
         caption = paste("Source: Ministry of Finance, revised 2024 workbook; directional principle.",
                         "ASEAN excl. Singapore = ASEAN total minus Singapore. Non-manufacturing includes services and other industries.",
                         sep = "\n")) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 18, base_family = "Arial") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 15),
          axis.text = element_text(colour = "black", size = 16),
          panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 17),
          plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0),
          plot.margin = margin(8, 16, 8, 8))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: japanese-fdi-major-destinations
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-alt: "Japanese outward FDI in 2024 to selected major destinations, including Singapore separately from ASEAN excluding Singapore, split into manufacturing and non-manufacturing."
fdi_destination_plot(
  c("United States", "United Kingdom", "Singapore", "ASEAN excl. Singapore", "Netherlands", "Australia", "India", "Germany", "China"),
  divisor = 10000, unit_label = "trillion yen",
  subtitle = "Selected major destinations, 2024", accuracy = 0.01
)
```

## Who invests in Japan?

```{r}
#| label: inward-fdi-sources
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-alt: "Selected sources of net inward FDI into Japan in 2024. Singapore is separate from ASEAN excluding Singapore. Germany has a negative net flow."
inward_sources = fdi_2024[direction == "Inward" & industry == "Total" &
  destination %in% c("Hong Kong", "Switzerland", "Singapore", "United Kingdom", "Taiwan",
                     "Netherlands", "France", "Canada", "China", "United States",
                     "Germany", "ASEAN excl. Singapore")]
inward_sources[, value_bn := value_100million_yen / 10]
setorder(inward_sources, value_bn)
inward_sources[, destination := factor(destination, levels = destination)]
ggplot(inward_sources, aes(value_bn, destination)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_col(fill = "#4477AA", width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, big.mark = ",")(value_bn),
                hjust = ifelse(value_bn < 0, 1.12, -0.12)), size = 4.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.16, 0.16))) +
  labs(x = "Annual net inward FDI (billion yen)", y = NULL,
       subtitle = "Selected source economies, 2024",
       caption = paste("Source: Ministry of Finance, revised 2024 workbook; directional principle.",
                       "Immediate counterpart economy. ASEAN excl. Singapore = ASEAN minus Singapore. Negative values = net withdrawals.", sep = "\n")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18, base_family = "Arial") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 15, colour = "black"),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0))
```


## Which industries attract FDI into Japan?

```{r}
#| label: inward-fdi-industries
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-alt: "Selected industries receiving inward FDI in Japan in 2024. Finance and insurance, communications and electric machinery have large positive net flows; wholesale and retail has a negative net flow."
inward_industries = fdi_2024[direction == "Inward" & destination == "World" &
  industry %in% c("Finance and insurance", "Communications", "Electric machinery", "Services",
                  "Chemicals and pharmaceuticals", "Real estate", "Transportation",
                  "Transportation equipment", "Wholesale and retail")]
inward_industries[, sector := ifelse(industry %in%
  c("Electric machinery", "Chemicals and pharmaceuticals", "Transportation equipment"),
  "Manufacturing", "Non-manufacturing")]
inward_industries[, value_bn := value_100million_yen / 10]
setorder(inward_industries, value_bn)
inward_industries[, industry := factor(industry, levels = industry)]
inward_manufacturing = fdi_2024[direction == "Inward" & destination == "World" & industry == "Manufacturing", value_100million_yen] / 10
inward_nonmanufacturing = fdi_2024[direction == "Inward" & destination == "World" & industry == "Non-manufacturing", value_100million_yen] / 10
ggplot(inward_industries, aes(value_bn, industry, fill = sector)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label_number(accuracy = 0.1, big.mark = ",")(value_bn),
                hjust = ifelse(value_bn < 0, 1.12, -0.12)), size = 4.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Manufacturing" = "#4477AA", "Non-manufacturing" = "#DDCC77")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.17, 0.17))) +
  labs(x = "Annual net inward FDI (billion yen)", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       subtitle = sprintf("2024 totals: manufacturing %.1f; non-manufacturing %.1f billion yen",
                          inward_manufacturing, inward_nonmanufacturing),
       caption = paste("Source: Ministry of Finance, revised 2024 workbook; directional principle. Selected industries.",
                       "Services is a narrow source category, not all services. Negative values = net withdrawals.", sep = "\n")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18, base_family = "Arial") +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 15, colour = "black"),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 14),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 15),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0))
```

## Japan's capital liberalization and FDI

- **Before the 1970s:** strict controls on capital transactions.
- **1970s:** gradual liberalization of inward direct and portfolio investment.
- **1980:** foreign exchange regime shifted from generally prohibited unless permitted to generally free unless restricted.
- **1980s–1990s:** further liberalization of outward investment and foreign borrowing.

::: notes
- Adapted from the capital controls and liberalization timeline in the Balance of Payments lecture.
- Legal openness does not automatically eliminate business costs, hiring difficulties, or other barriers.
:::

## Barriers to inward FDI

<div class="slide-font-size" style="--slide-font-size: 65%">

| Reported barrier | 2012 (%) | 2016 (%) |
|---|---:|---:|
| High cost of doing business | 78.6 | 74.6 |
| Distinctiveness of the Japanese market | 43.1 | 46.6 |
| Difficulty securing personnel | 34.1 | 45.7 |
| Strict regulations and permits | 36.7 | 32.1 |
| Complicated administrative procedures | 33.7 | 28.6 |

Source: Hoshi (2018), Table 1, based on METI surveys of foreign affiliates.

</div>

::: notes
- These are selected responses from the 2012 and 2016 surveys, not a comprehensive ranking of all barriers.
- The reported difficulty securing personnel increased between surveys.
- Connect this Japan case to the broader regulatory, infrastructure and institutional barriers in the next slide.
:::

## Japan's inward FDI and business environment

```{r}
# Data used in the Balance of Payments lecture; place a copy at this relative path.
fdi_business = fread("../data/08 fdi/fdi_dtf.csv")
reference_countries = c("Luxembourg", "Ireland", "Netherlands", "United States", "China", "Argentina", "Brazil", "Korea")
ggplot(fdi_business, aes(Inward_FDI, Business_Index)) +
  geom_point(color = "gray70") +
  geom_point(data = fdi_business[Country == "Japan"], color = "red", size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = fdi_business[Country == "Japan"], aes(label = Country), vjust = -1, color = "red") +
  geom_text(data = fdi_business[Country %in% reference_countries], aes(label = Country), vjust = -1, color = "gray40", size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Inward FDI (% of GDP, log; 2015–2024 average)", y = "Doing Business Score (log; 2019–2020 average)", caption = "Source: OECD, World Bank; adapted from Balance of Payments lecture") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16, base_family = "Arial") +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0))
```

::: notes
- The original lecture emphasizes Japan's relatively low inward FDI compared with other advanced economies.
- This is a descriptive cross-country comparison, not evidence that the business score causes FDI.
:::


## Investment logic: FDI vs. ODA

<div class="slide-font-size" style="--slide-font-size: 60%">
| **Aspect** | **Commercial FDI** | **Strategic investment** | **ODA** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Main actor** | Private firms (MNEs) | State-linked firms, state-backed investors | Official agencies |
| **Objective** | Profit, market access, efficiency | Supply security, influence, geopolitical position | Development and welfare of recipients |
| **Terms** | Market-based returns | Returns may be secondary to strategic gain | Concessional (grant element) |
| **Risk appetite** | Avoids high-risk, low-return locations | May accept lower returns for strategic reasons | Goes where private capital avoids |
| **Link to recipient** | Follows investment climate | Shapes it to its own ends | Builds preconditions for investment |
</div>

::: notes
- Table is a framing device; adapt the "strategic" column to the cases you plan to discuss.
:::

## ODA and FDI relationship

::: {.slide-font-size style="--slide-font-size: 100%; line-height:1.45; width:100%;"}

- **Infrastructure and human capital improvement**<br>
  → lower investment costs

- **Institutional reforms and risk reduction**<br>
  → improved investment climate

- **Policy dialogue and technical cooperation**<br>
  → regulatory harmonization

:::

## Vietnam: FDI and ODA

```{r}
#| label: vietnam-fdi-oda
#| dev: ragg_png
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-alt: "Vietnam's implemented FDI and net ODA received, 1991-2019, with their shares of gross fixed capital formation from 1994."
vietnam = fread("../data/08 fdi/vietnam_fdi_oda_1991_2019.csv")

vietnam_flows = melt(
  vietnam,
  id.vars = "year",
  measure.vars = c("fdi_implemented_usd_million", "net_oda_received_usd_million"),
  variable.name = "flow", value.name = "amount"
)
vietnam_flows[, flow := factor(flow,
  levels = c("fdi_implemented_usd_million", "net_oda_received_usd_million"),
  labels = c("FDI", "ODA"))]

# Recalculate shares from the amounts; keep unavailable GFCF years missing.
vietnam_shares = melt(
  vietnam[!is.na(gfcf_usd_million) & gfcf_usd_million > 0,
    .(year,
      `FDI / GFCF` = 100 * fdi_implemented_usd_million / gfcf_usd_million,
      `ODA / GFCF` = 100 * net_oda_received_usd_million / gfcf_usd_million)],
  id.vars = "year", variable.name = "series", value.name = "share"
)

# Map 0-60% on the right axis onto 0-25,000 million USD on the left.
share_axis_scale = 25000 / 60
ggplot() +
  geom_col(data = vietnam_flows,
           aes(year, amount, fill = flow),
           position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = vietnam_shares,
            aes(year, share * share_axis_scale, colour = series), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FDI" = "#3D3052", "ODA" = "#E96A00")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FDI / GFCF" = "#FF8B3D", "ODA / GFCF" = "#8060A6")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1991:2019, expand = expansion(add = 0.6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Million current US$", limits = c(0, 25000),
    breaks = seq(0, 25000, 5000), labels = label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02)),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . / share_axis_scale,
                        name = "Share of GFCF", breaks = seq(0, 60, 10),
                        labels = label_number(suffix = "%"))
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(order = 1), colour = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, fill = NULL, colour = NULL,
       caption = paste(
         "Sources: Vietnam NSO series via JP-VN; archived World Bank/OECD series via IndexMundi.",
         "FDI = implemented capital; ODA = net aid from all donors. GFCF shares available from 1994.",
         sep = "\n")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18, base_family = "Arial") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.box = "horizontal",
        legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1, size = 13),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 14),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0),
        plot.margin = margin(8, 12, 8, 8))
```


## Complementary vs. Substitution

- Complementary view:
  - ODA builds preconditions for private investment (infrastructure, governance).
  - Especially in low-income countries where private capital avoids risk.

- Substitution view:
  - Excessive aid can crowd out FDI if it distorts markets or maintains uncompetitive sectors.
  - Conditional or tied aid may limit spillovers.

## Japan’s Experience

<div class="slide-font-size" style="--slide-font-size: 80%">
- Tied aid and “ingredients approach” → enabled Japanese firms to invest later.
- Evidence: Ono and Sekiyama (2023) on the effect of ODA on FDI by aid type
- Case study: Vietnam (Tsuno, 2023)
- Transition from aid-recipient to investment-partner relationship.
</div>


## Discussions

<div class="slide-font-size" style="--slide-font-size: 80%">
1. Is it a problem that Japan’s outward FDI is about six times its inward FDI? Yes, no, or it depends?

2. Japan removed most legal restrictions on inward FDI decades ago, but inward FDI is still low. Looking at the METI survey table, which barrier could the government actually fix, and which could it not?

3. Private investors avoid risky, low-return countries, but ODA goes there. How could ODA make a country like Vietnam more attractive to private investors?

4. Japan’s tied aid helped Japanese firms invest later. Is that good development cooperation or aid serving the donor’s interests?
</div>
